failures.title: Volkswagen CRLB Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: AdBlue System and NOx Sensor Failures - 2012-2019 models
items.whatHappens: The EA288 Gen 3 relies heavily on AdBlue injection for Euro 6 compliance. Heater elements within the AdBlue tank and the downstream NOx sensors are prone to failure. This triggers an "Emissions Malfunction" warning on the dashboard and frequently forces the vehicle into limp mode, restricting power and preventing engine restarts after a certain mileage countdown.
items.repairVsReplace: If the engine block and internals are healthy, replacing the AdBlue tank/sensor assembly (£400-£1,500) is the correct fix. However, if chronic AdBlue crystallisation has caused secondary overheating or EGR cooler leaks, a full Volkswagen CRLB engine replacement becomes the more reliable long-term solution. Read our full AdBlue system failure guide.

items.title: DPF Clogging (Urban Use) - All CRLB variants
items.whatHappens: Frequent short trips prevent the Diesel Particulate Filter from reaching the high temperatures required for active regeneration. Soot builds up, increasing exhaust backpressure. Over time, this restricts airflow, leading to turbocharger strain, reduced performance, and potential oil dilution as unburnt fuel washes past the piston rings.
items.repairVsReplace: A professional DPF clean or forced regeneration can resolve early-stage clogging. If the DPF is physically cracked or the turbo has suffered oil starvation due to blocked return lines, a reconditioned CRLB engine is often more cost-effective than piecemeal component replacement. Read our full DPF clogging guide.

failures.goodYearsLine: The CRLB (EA288 Gen 3) is generally considered significantly more robust than its predecessor, the EA189, with timing chain issues being far less prevalent. Post-2015 software updates also improved AdBlue dosing reliability, making later-model CRLB units a safer bet .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the CRLB
variants.intro: The Volkswagen CRLB engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, located on a machined pad near the junction of the engine and the transmission bell housing. It is also clearly listed on your V5C registration document under "Engine Number" and can be decoded from your 17-digit VIN.

relatives.description: - The earlier EA189 common-rail variant that preceded the CRLB, lacking the updated Euro 6 AdBlue architecture but sharing similar DPF sensitivities.

- The exact same physical EA288 2.0 TDI unit fitted to contemporary Audi A3, A4, and Q5 models, sharing identical failure patterns and replacement economics.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Volkswagen CRLB - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Volkswagen CRLB engine is a viable option only if it comes with a verifiable service history proving regular oil changes and a recent DPF/AdBlue system health check. Without this documentation, you risk inheriting hidden carbon buildup or failing NOx sensors that will trigger limp mode shortly after installation. Explore vetted options via our used engines network.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned CRLB is the recommended choice for most owners. A reputable rebuild will include a refreshed turbocharger, new EGR and AdBlue components, and a cleaned or replaced DPF, directly addressing the EA288's known weak points and restoring the engine to near-factory reliability. Compare reconditioned engines today.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-mileage CRLB units that have suffered secondary damage, such as turbo failure leading to oil starvation or severe AdBlue crystallisation damaging the block. An upgraded rebuild should include revised piston rings and an updated water pump assembly to prevent future coolant leaks. Learn more about rebuilt engines.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Opting for a supply-and-fit service through our network ensures the replacement is performed by Volkswagen specialists, with the warranty backed by the installing garage for complete peace of mind. View our supply and fit options.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The CRLB is typically found in Volkswagen Golf Mk7, Passat B8, and Tiguan models valued between £4,000 and £18,000 . For lower-value examples (sub-£5,000), a reconditioned engine costing £2,800+ may approach or exceed 60% of the vehicle's current market value. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the CRLB engine?
items.answer: The most frequent documented issue with the Volkswagen CRLB is AdBlue system failure, specifically NOx sensor or heater malfunctions. This triggers an "Emissions Malfunction" warning and can force the vehicle into limp mode. DPF clogging from frequent short urban trips is the second most common failure pattern.

items.answer: The CRLB is widely fitted across mainstream Volkswagen models from 2012 to 2019, most notably the Golf Mk7, Passat B8, and Tiguan. It was also used in the Volkswagen Sharan Mk2 during this period. Always verify your specific fitment using your registration number before ordering parts.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned CRLB engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Volkswagen CRLB is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known risks of inherited AdBlue and DPF issues. Used engines carry a 3-6 month warranty and may have undocumented urban wear. Reconditioned units include refreshed emission components and a 12-24 month warranty.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the CRLB engine?
items.answer: The CRLB engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block, near the transmission bell housing, and is listed on your V5C registration document. It is commonly confused with earlier EA189 codes like CRBC or later CNHA variants. Fitting the wrong revision can cause ECU mapping and turbo plumbing mismatches.
